Report: Goldman Sachs Predicts the S&P 500 Will Gain 26% in 12 Months
Despite a rocky few weeks on Wall Street, the next 12 months are looking much more bullish, according to Goldman Sachs.
By Ben Gran –
Key Points
- Research from the Wall Street firm predicts that the S&P 500 will climb to 8,700 in the next 12 months, for a gain of about 26% from Friday's close.
- Goldman strategists believe that valuations of tech stocks and AI hyperscalers have reached attractive levels after their recent sell-off.
- The S&P 500 forward price-to-earnings ratio is at a 15% discount compared to its past five-year average.
The stock market has had a rough few weeks. As of Nov. 20, the S&P 500 index (^GSPC -3.70%) had declined by about 10.4% in the prior month, largely driven by investor worries over the sustainability of the artificial intelligence (AI) trade. The tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 index has declined almost enough to qualify as a bear market, with a drop of nearly 20% since its Oct. 6 record high.
But according to Bloomberg reporting from Nov. 13, Goldman Sachs (GS -6.71%) strategists are bullish on the S&P 500 for next year. Recent research from Goldman suggests that the benchmark S&P index will gain 26% in the next 12 months by November 2027, despite possibly lower earnings growth compared to 2026.
Let's look at what this might mean for investors -- and why it's a good sign to keep buying stocks with low-cost index funds like S&P 500 ETFs.
Image source: Getty Images.
Goldman's forecast for the S&P 500 by the end of 2027
Goldman strategists predict that the S&P 500 will reach 8,700 points in the next 12 months. On Nov. 20, the index closed at about 6,910, so this would imply a gain of about 26% from that level.
That's not an outlandish return to expect for the S&P 500. A 26% gain in 12 months would be an exceptionally strong year, much better than the average. But it's well within the realm of possibility.
Keep in mind that the long-term average annual return for the S&P 500, based on historical data since 1928, is 9.98%. And in the past few years, the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -3.42%) has delivered annual returns of about 17.8% in 2025, 25% in 2024, and 26.3% in 2023.

Why does Goldman think the S&P 500 will do so well in the next 12 months? If so many investors are nervous about tech companies spending too much on AI data centers, isn't now a bad time to buy the S&P? After all, as of Nov. 19, eight of the top 10 holdings in the S&P 500 were tech names, and those top eight stocks made up about 33.5% of the index by weight.
The answer is in the valuations.
Tech stock valuations have become cheaper
Recent investor skepticism about AI stocks might actually be healthy for future returns. Recent declines in tech stock prices have driven down those companies' valuations. Goldman's research finds that AI hyperscalers are trading "well below" their historic valuations and says that "we see Technology -- and Hyperscalers in particular -- as relatively defensive."
The very same tech stocks that have been going through a correction in the past month might be poised for bigger gains in the next 12 months. Goldman says that even though some of the biggest hyperscalers have negative cash flow due to their aggressive AI investments, these companies still have strong balance sheets and could become attractive in the next 12 months if growth opportunities elsewhere are harder to find.

When Cameron Balser arrived at New York City Hall at 11:45 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on November 20, 2026, he set a new speed record for the Trans America Run, a route stretching from San Francisco, California, on the West Coast, to New York City on the East Coast and covering 3,067 miles (4,935 kilometers).
He’d been running on the route, affectionately called the “TransAm,” for 41 days, 16 hours, and 45 minutes, and he was joined by a large crowd on the streets of New York City to celebrate his accomplishment.
When Balser left the San Francisco City Hall at 5:00 a.m. Pacific Daylight Time, on October 10, he was chasing Pete Kostelnick’s record from 2016. Kostelnick ran between the city halls in 42 days, 6 hours, and 30 minutes. With seemingly the tightest of margins for a run of this length, Balser broke Kostelnick’s time by 13 hours and 45 minutes.
He’d covered more than 140,000 feet of elevation gain while traversing across California, Nevada, Utah, Colorado, Nebraska, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and finally New York, and averaged 73.61 miles per day. Running over mountains, through deserts and prairies, and everything in between, Basler’s consistency over all types of terrain was impressive, both with his efficient crew and his steady pace.
Across the Country
The 35-year-old Indiana native named his run “Breaking 42,” making his intentions to run farther than Kostelnick’s 72.56-mile daily average clear from the start. Winter weather delays in the Rockies complicated Balser’s plans early on, including a forced early stop due to rain that made a dirt road impassable for support-vehicle access and snow at the high point of his route, Cameron Pass, in Colorado.
With remarkable consistency, Balser broke his 15- to 16-hour days into five-mile segments, taking in around 800 calories at each crew stop to keep his energy levels up. He aimed to run every uphill stretch to finish each day’s mileage as efficiently as possible.
Once out of the Colorado mountains, Balser went on to surge across the prairies, cranking out 75-mile days through the flatter terrain of the Midwest and East Coast as he closed in on New York. Throughout the route, he was joined by friends and fans, and he kept a live tracker available for anyone who wanted to share miles with him.
Unlike a fixed trail fastest known time where the route is defined, the Trans America Run record is defined by its endpoints — the San Francisco City Hall and New York City Hall — and Balser’s crew spent months studying Kostelnick’s 2016 blueprint, even joking on social media that they were “sick and tired of studying [his] route/record.”
Prior record holder Kostelnick cheered Balser on throughout his attempt. A couple of days before Balser’s finish, he quipped on social media: “It’s always humbling to see a record you put so (damn) much into get broken, but I’ve learned it also requires genuine appreciation for the person willing to chase your ghost. To really recognize them, especially when they’ve done it the right way. San Francisco to NYC. Showing happiness over clicks. Give us more of that, Cameron.”
On the final night, Balser was joined by several dozen runners for the last 11 miles in from the George Washington Bridge. With only a mile left, he clearly relished the cheers from onlookers, stating calmly, “That was a good run.” He walked the final mile to the finish, smiling under the New York City lights. This Dividend ETF Could Supercharge Your Passive Income. Here's How.
Most income investors trade growth for yield. This ETF lets you have both.
By Keith Speights –
Key Points
- The Goldman Sachs S&P 500 Core Premium Income ETF holds S&P 500 stocks and sells call options on 25% to 75% of the portfolio to generate income.
- It has paid an 8.3% distribution yield over the past year while delivering average annual returns of 20.4% since its 2023 launch.
- The ETF is best for income investors who want some growth.
Many income investors view the trade-off between high yields and growth potential as a necessary evil. They think having both is virtually impossible.
However, that doesn't have to be the case. The Goldman Sachs S&P 500 Core Premium Income ETF (GPIX -3.38%) offers both high yields and growth. This dividend ETF could be the passive income and growth engine that many investors didn't know existed.
Image source: Getty Images.
What sets this ETF apart
Like several top S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%) index funds, the Goldman Sachs S&P 500 Core Premium Income ETF provides exposure to the S&P 500. Its top holdings include the largest components of the S&P 500 index itself: Apple (AAPL -1.90%), Microsoft (MSFT -2.77%), Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%), Amazon (AMZN -4.10%), and Alphabet (GOOG -2.59%) (GOOGL -2.70%).
But this isn't an ordinary S&P 500 ETF. Two words in the fund's name hint at what sets it apart: "Premium Income." The Goldman Sachs S&P 500 Core Premium Income ETF paid a distribution yield of 8.3% over the last 12 months. That's roughly eight times the yields offered by the State Street SPDR® S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY -3.64%) and the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO -3.42%).
How does this ETF generate such juicy distributions? It uses a dynamic options "overwrite" strategy. What that means is that the Goldman Sachs fund sells call options on some, but not all, of its equity investments -- usually between 25% and 75%.
The fund's managers sell more call options to generate greater premium income when they view the market's upside as limited. And they dial back the option selling when they expect the stock market to rally.
This approach allows the Goldman Sachs S&P 500 Core Premium Income ETF to generate both growth and income. Since its inception in October 2023, the fund has delivered an average annual total return of 20.4%, not far below the S&P 500's 22.7%. But it has also given shareholders significantly higher income than the S&P 500 has.

Missouri livestock farmers face environmental regulations. The CAFO debate should reflect that.
(Scott Olson/Getty Images)
A recent commentary in the Missouri Independent by Rural Crisis Center member Darvin Bentlage paints a misleading picture of Missouri’s livestock industry and the environmental safeguards that govern it.
Missouri’s livestock producers supply affordable, domestically produced protein while operating under state and federal environmental regulations designed to protect our natural resources. Those safeguards deserve to be part of the discussion.
The suggestion that Missouri livestock producers operate with virtually no environmental oversight overlooks important requirements already in place. Concentrated animal feeding operations (CAFOs) are subject to extensive state and federal environmental requirements governing facility construction, manure storage, nutrient management, land application and water quality. Requirements vary by the size and type of operation.
Missouri’s CAFO policy is built to multiply pollution, not prevent it
These are not voluntary suggestions. They are enforceable regulations, and producers must comply or face penalties.
Start with the numbers. The commentary claims Missouri’s impaired waters list grew from 24 in 2002 to 549 today.But those figures do not provide a straightforward comparison of water quality over time. The state’s current list includes 24 impairments first identified in 2002, not a total of just 24 impairments that year.
The commentary also points to 215 listings added since 2020. An important part of the explanation is a change in how Missouri evaluates water quality. Missouri adopted numeric nutrient criteria for lakes in 2018, and the 2020 list was the first to be measured against those criteria.The new standards led to additional lakes being identified as impaired.
That is not evidence that livestock farms are driving a surge in pollution. Rather, as standards become more protective, more waters may be added to the impaired waters list. In fact, none of the 549 listings identifies a CAFO or livestock farm as its source.
The commentary also suggests that Missouri has no meaningful setback requirements. While Missouri does not require minimum spacing between separate CAFOs, other siting protections exist. Missouri regulations establish minimum separation distances. For example, CAFOs must be more than facilities generally must be at least 100 feet from human water supply lakes, losing streams or sinkholes. Larger operations are also subject to substantial buffer distances (in some cases, more than half a mile) from neighboring residences and public buildings, along with advance neighbor notification requirements. These safeguards exist for a reason: to protect neighboring landowners and natural resources while allowing responsible agricultural operations to continue.
Missouri’s approach to CAFO regulation recognizes that responsible facility siting involves far more than the distance between neighboring operations. Livestock operations must account for their surroundings, comply with established applicable engineering standards and meet environmental requirements.
Missouri’s regulatory framework includes setbacks from waterways and residences, though it does not establish minimum distances between separate CAFOs. Those existing safeguards are an important part of evaluating whether additional requirements are warranted.

Doing his best impersonation of the fictional movie protagonist who developed a passion for running, Balser, a 35-year-old red-bearded and straggly-haired ultrarunner from Indiana, spent the past six weeks spreading messages of love, joy, and kindness on an epic quest to run across the U.S. in record time.

After running a few brisk miles through Manhattan, he eventually met up with his mom, stepdad, and two sisters and slowed to a walk on the final few blocks on the way to his finishing point.

So instead, he walked to a point adjacent to City Hall and, like Gump mythically did in Monument Valley, Utah, he just stopped.
Balser officially ended his relentless push across the country at 11:45 p.m., which means he covered the 3,067-mile journey in a record-breaking 41 days, 16 hours, and 45 minutes—roughly 13 hours and 45 minutes faster than Kostelnick.

A powerful stride depends on having a strong core. It’s basically the glue that holds your running form together and will make every mile more efficient, helping you hit faster speeds.
But between fitting in runs, setting aside time for recovery, fueling, and living life outside of running shoes, it’s hard to know if you’re dedicating enough time to strengthening this key muscle group. So when your calendar is already packed, what’s the minimum number of core workouts you need to do to reap the benefits?
We asked experts for that magic minimum number, so you can boost your performance without carving a ton of time out of your busy schedule.
The Minimum Amount of Core Work Runners Need
Simply put, every runner should aim to get at least two 10- to 15-minute core sessions done per week, says Yusuf Jeffers, NYC-based strength and run coach, Hyrox race director, and Nike Well Collective trainer. This is an adequate number to support your running form, build more strength and power, and improve overall running efficiency.
However, several factors can adjust this number, including your running goals and the season you’re in, says Holly Dickinson, UESCA-certified run coach, NSCA-certified strength and conditioning coach, and owner of StrideHer run coaching. For example, if building strength is your offseason goal and you’re not running as much mileage as you would during race training, you might increase the minimum amount of core work you do to three or four sessions per week. During a racing season, though, you might stick to two sessions per week.
As for the exercises you need, you can skip moves like crunches, which can stress your back and neck muscles and isolate just a few ab muscles (namely, the rectus abdominis or those six-pack abs) and instead, go for moves like planks, bird dogs, Copenhagen side planks, and glute bridges. These moves help with spinal and pelvic stability and core muscular endurance, and mimic running form—plus, they work 360 degrees of your core.
Jeffers recommends spending at least 30 seconds on each move, completing your core work in a circuit-style fashion (which means completing each move back-to-back with minimal rest in between) and repeating the circuit for at least two sets.
If you strength train regularly, you probably don’t have to do any additional core workouts because many programs often require you to brace your midsection and keep your spine neutral in order to do the exercise properly, Jeffers adds, which is basically like built-in core work. Think of weighted back squats, deadlifts, and bench presses, for example. You need to engage your core to maintain a stable spine through all of these exercises.
Why Runners Need Regular Core Work
Many people tend to think of the core as just ab muscles, but your core is literally everything that’s not your arms and legs, says Jeffers. That’s essentially everything from your abdominal muscles to your glutes, pelvic floor, and back. All of these muscles work together to keep you stable on your runs and prevent form breakdown.

The qualified-dividend rate grows with income. On top of it, the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT) applies above $200,000 of income for single filers and $250,000 for joint filers.
For joint filers, the 24% bracket covers taxable income from $211,400 to $403,550. That means many couples in the 24% bracket also owe the NIIT, which puts them in the 18.8% row. Congress sets these rates, and income inside a Roth is protected from any future change to them.

Invested back the $1,640 annual savings at a conservative 3%, and it grows to about $18,800 after 10 years and $44,067 after 20. Without reinvestment, the 20-year total is $32,800. On Thursday, November 19, 2026, Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META | META Price Prediction) posted its 2026 Sustainability Report and said it is rethinking the 2030 deadline for its net-zero goal. Its 2025 net emissions rose to 11.8 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent, up 45% from 2024.
The stock closed Friday, November 20, at $560.84, down 5.93%. That drop came during a broad tech selloff. Shares fell 11.6% over the past week, then traded at $569.32 after hours.
If you own the stock, what the report measures matters more than the climate headline, because Meta wrote it and it is one of the few direct measurements of how physical the AI expansion has become.
What Meta Committed To
Meta set the goal in 2020: net zero across its whole value chain, plus water positive, by 2030. The report opens with a letter. In it, Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability, wrote that Meta is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones.”
They said AI demand grew faster than almost anyone projected, and clean energy fell behind because of years-long grid interconnection waiting lines, slow permitting, and lagging transmission. Meta says its long-term dreams are unchanged, but it gave no date for a revised plan.
How Emissions Jumped 45% on 100% Clean Power
Meta says it matched 100% of its electricity with clean and renewable energy for the sixth straight year. Direct Scope 1 emissions were just 33,555 tons, and market-based Scope 2 (purchased power) was 10,861 tons.
Almost all of the footprint is Scope 3, the emissions in Meta’s supply chain. Scope 3 amounted to 11,858,913 tons, about 99% of the total. Capital goods such as servers, chips, networking gear, steel and concrete made up 73%, and clean power contracts do little to reduce them.
Emissions Double as a Capex Gauge
Capital goods emissions rise with physical construction, so this footprint tracks spending. By our calculation, electricity use rose 34.9% to 24,849,122 megawatt-hours, and data centers used 24,523,035 of that. All of that steel, concrete, and power has to come from somebody, and we profiled seven of the suppliers behind the AI expansion in a free report.
Third-quarter capex was $34.906 billion[1], up 85.38%, and free cash flow was -$2.120 billion. Meta still guides 2026 capex to $135 billion to $145 billion[1].
That puts Meta’s interim Scope 3 target out of reach. By our math, 2025 Scope 3 was about 2.05 times the 5,772,583-ton 2021 baseline Meta aims not to exceed by end-2031. Reaching it would require cleaner suppliers or slower building.
Power Limits Threaten the AI Plan Itself
The interconnection waiting lines and permitting delays that slowed clean energy also limit how fast new data centers can come online. Mark Zuckerberg spoke on the October 21, 2026[2] earnings call. He said Muse is “very compute-intensive to run”[2] and that “we have not launched it globally yet.”
Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG, NASDAQ:GOOGL), Google’s parent company, faces the same pressure. It pledged in 2020 to run on carbon-free energy by 2030, stopped saying carbon-neutral operations by 2024, and has acknowledged that its emissions are still rising.

On a late November day on the U.S. East Coast, Americans Sydney Welch and Coleman Cragun took home wins in the JFK 50 Mile, one of the oldest and most historic ultramarathons in the U.S. Cragun gained some separation after the initial Appalachian Trail section and held off several fast runners in the flatter final 35 miles to finish in 5:29:13, while Welch put in an incredibly impressive performance to finish in 6:04:03, the second-fastest time in race history.
Several hours earlier, at 6:30 a.m. Eastern Standard Time on Saturday, November 21, Cragun and Welch toed the start line in Boonsboro, Maryland, with 1,122 other runners to begin their 50-mile journey to Williamsport. Now in its 64th edition, the race attracts some of the top distance runners — ultrarunners, road marathoners, and everyone in between — hunting a fast 50-mile time on a storied course. The weather was typical of late fall on the East Coast — cloudy, with temperatures in the 40s Fahrenheit — perfect for fast racing.
The course starts with a 2.5-mile paved section before connecting with the Appalachian Trail and climbs nearly 1,200 feet in the first 5.3 miles, accounting for most of the course’s elevation gain. The 13-mile trail section is famously rocky and rooty, suiting runners with more trail experience, and then drops more than 1,000 feet in the last two miles of trail. At mile 15.5, runners exit the trail and end up on the C&O Canal Towpath, a fast and flat 26.3-mile section of gravel and dirt where runners can really start to move. Spectators and commentators alike like to analyze splits on this section, as it’s nearly equivalent to a marathon time. For the last eight-plus miles, runners traverse rolling country roads to the finish in Williamsport. It is, for these reasons, one of the true road-to-trail (or trail-to-road) races on the ultra calendar.
The race, which brings together elite and everyday runners, is steeped in American history. Inspired by former President Theodore Roosevelt, who, during his presidency in the early 1900s, required his military officers to cover 50 miles on foot in 20 hours, former President John F. Kennedy established a series of 50-mile races across the country for his own officers and any civilians seeking an endurance challenge. The first edition of the JFK 50 Mile took place in 1963, and it is now the only race from Kennedy’s original series that is still held every year. With the most prestigious award, the Kennedy Cup, awarded to the fastest military team, the race retains and celebrates its strong military roots.
2026 JFK 50 Mile Women’s Race
With none of last year’s top five returning, the race to be the women’s champion was wide open. Canada’s Maïka Lamoureux, sixth last year, was the top returner, while Courtney Olsen, the American 100k record holder and current 100k world champion, was making her JFK debut. Stephanie Bruce, who has three U.S. road running titles to her name, two in the 10k and another in the half marathon, was also expected to contend. A strong mix of more trail-focused runners, including Americans Sydney Welch and Tay Cavett and Canadian Élisa Morin, made it a compelling and hard-to-predict race.

Meta Stopped Its Buybacks To Build AI. How Much More Can It Spend?
Today’s big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks?
Meta has stopped buying back its own stock. It spent $26 billion on buybacks in the first nine months of 2025. In the same months of 2026, it spent nothing. The cash went into capital spending, the money a company puts into long-lived assets such as data centers. So how much more can Meta spend in 2027? And what would that mean for Nvidia?
Friday, Nov 20, was a hard day for AI stocks. Nvidia fell 14.0% and the Nasdaq 100 fund (QQQ) 5.7%. Meta fell 5.9%, more than the S&P 500 fund (SPY), which lost 3.6%.
Where Meta’s cash came from and where it went
Source: Trefis, from Meta’s cash-flow statements for the first nine months of each year. Interest is from its income statements.
Meta’s business brought in $97 billion in those nine months. That is $17 billion more than a year earlier. It put $83 billion of it into capital spending. That is 86 cents of every dollar, up from 61 cents.
Meta also borrowed $25 billion. Its debt rose from $29 billion a year earlier to $84 billion. In November it sold another $15 billion and €9 billion of bonds. In late October it sold about $14 billion of preferred stock that converts into shares. It also agreed to sell 40 million new shares by November 2027. Its interest bill more than tripled, to $2.3 billion. That is still small next to the $97 billion of cash its business brought in.
Meta’s buybacks went from $26 billion to zero in a year. If you are waiting to see whether that spending works before you buy, your cash does not have to sit idle. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500’s, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays.
This piece is one of our looks at the cash of the biggest AI buyers. Our overview of all five is Big Tech Earned $607 Billion. Where Did It Go?
Can Meta Spend More Next Year?
Yes. About $31 billion more from its own cash.
Analysts expect Meta’s sales to reach $313 billion in 2027. Meta turns 55 cents of every $1 of sales into cash. That would bring in about $172 billion.
Source: Trefis. Sales are the 2027 consensus forecast of 45 analysts. Cash is figured at 55 cents per $1 of sales, Meta’s rate over the past four quarters. Dividends are at the latest quarter’s rate. The last line counts borrowing until debt equals a year of cash, from $83.7 billion of borrowed debt at Sep 30, leases excluded.
So Meta can raise its spending about 23% from its current pace. That assumes no new debt and no buybacks. Its room to borrow is the smallest of the three cash-rich buyers, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta. That is because its debt nearly tripled in the past year. The bonds it sold in November, about $25 billion, cut that room to about $64 billion. We run the same numbers for Microsoft in Microsoft Was The Only Big AI Buyer Paying Down Debt. How Much More Can It Spend?
What Would Nvidia Get?
About $16 billion from Meta’s own cash. Up to $63 billion if Meta borrows.
Nvidia’s sales equal about 52 cents of every $1 the five biggest buyers spend. On that measure, Meta’s $31 billion of room is worth about $16 billion to Nvidia. With borrowing, Meta’s room is $120 billion. That is worth about $63 billion to Nvidia. Even so, about $118 billion of analysts’ forecast for Nvidia is not yet covered by any buyer’s cash or borrowing room.
